etymology: Webster 1828 treats MOUNT as noun from Latin mons, a heap or elevation: a mass of earth or rock rising above the surrounding land, used in Scripture both of Sinai and of small hillocks of witness (Genesis 31). Also a mound or bulwark (Jeremiah 6:6). As verb: to rise, to ascend, to get upon an elevated place. This page fills the KJV-gap common of the height where God meets man. Companion pages already treat sinai, zion, and covenant.
biblical_def: Mount in Scripture is not a scenic overlook and not a self-made high place. It is the elevation God names, comes down upon, and forbids men to climb in their own fire. The LORD came down upon mount Sinai and called Moses up (Exo 19:20). Trust is not a mood: they that trust in the LORD shall be as mount Zion, which cannot be removed (Psa 125:1). The new covenant will not send you back to the mount that might be touched and that burned with fire (Heb 12:18). You are come unto mount Sion, and unto the city of the living God (Heb 12:22). Moses abode in the mount forty days to receive the tables of the covenant (Deu 9:9). The dictionary therefore keeps mount from becoming either tourism or a throne of the heart. It is the Bible’s way of saying: God descends, or you do not arrive.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines MOUNT as noun: a mass of earth or rock rising above the surrounding land; a mound or bulwark; formerly a bank of money. Verb intransitive: to rise on high; to ascend; to tower; to get on horseback. Verb transitive: to raise aloft; to climb; to furnish with horses; to carry guns. He cites Genesis 31, Jeremiah 6:6, Job 39:27, and Jeremiah 51:53.
webster_full: MOUNT, noun [Latin mons, literally a heap or an elevation.]

1. A mass of earth, or earth and rock, rising considerably above the common surface of the surrounding land. mount is used for an eminence or elevation of earth, indefinite in highth or size, and may be a hillock, hill or mountain. We apply it to mount Blanc, in Switzerland, to mount Tom and mount Holyoke, in Massachusetts, and it is applied in Scripture to the small hillocks on which sacrifice was offered as well as to mount Sinai. Jacob offered sacrifice on the mount or heap of stones raised for a witness between him and Laban. Genesis 31:21.
2. A mound; a bulwark for offense or defense.
Hew ye down trees and cast a mount against Jerusalem. Jeremiah 6:6.
MOUNT, verb intransitive
1. To rise on high; to ascend; with or without up.
Doth the eagle mount up at thy command? Job 39:27.
2. To rise; to ascend; to tower; to be built to a great altitude.
Though Babylon should mount up to heaven. Jeremiah 51:53.
MOUNT, verb transitive To raise aloft; to lift on high.
1. To ascend; to climb; to get upon an elevated place; as, to mount a throne.
scriptures: And the LORD came down upon mount Sinai, on the top of the mount: and the LORD called Moses up to the top of the mount; and Moses went up.
A Song of degrees. They that trust in the LORD shall be as mount Zion, which cannot be removed, but abideth for ever.
For ye are not come unto the mount that might be touched, and that burned with fire, nor unto blackness, and darkness, and tempest,
But ye are come unto mount Sion, and unto the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to an innumerable company of angels,
Deu 9:9

When I was gone up into the mount to receive the tables of stone, even the tables of the covenant which the LORD made with you, then I abode in the mount forty days and forty nights, I neither did eat bread nor drink water:
corruption_summary: Mount is corrupted when Sinai is recast as a wellness retreat, when Zion is sold as a political brand, and when men mount their own thrones and call the climb piety.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is Sinai as scenery. Exodus 19:20 is the LORD coming down, not a hike with a view. The age keeps the mountain and drops the fire. Tourism is not covenant.

The second corruption is Zion as a slogan. Psalm 125:1 trusts in the LORD and is as mount Zion. The recovery is not a flag. Hebrews 12:22 is come unto mount Sion, the city of the living God — not a campaign stop.

The third corruption is the heart that mounts. Isaiah 14:13 would sit upon the mount of the congregation. Hebrews 12:18 says ye are not come unto the mount that might be touched. Self-exaltation is not ascent.

etymology: Webster 1828 treats NEAR as adjective: nigh; not far distant in place, time, or degree; closely related by blood; present and ready to aid (Isaiah 55:6); intimate. As adverb: almost. As verb: to approach (a seaman’s phrase). This page fills the KJV-gap common of proximity under God. Companion pages already treat draw, come, and prayer.
biblical_def: Near in Scripture is not a vibe and not a GPS pin. It is the LORD who may be called while He is near, and the sinner who is commanded to draw near with a true heart. Asaph will not keep God at arm’s length: it is good for me to draw near to God (Psa 73:28). The prophet will not postpone mercy: call ye upon him while he is near (Isa 55:6). The Lord will not leave the last days as a calendar hobby: know that it is near, even at the doors (Mat 24:33). The new covenant will not baptize a distant religiosity: let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith (Heb 10:22). Salvation is not receding: now is our salvation nearer than when we believed (Rom 13:11). The dictionary therefore keeps near from becoming either slack intimacy or a postponed appointment. It is the Bible’s way of saying: He is at hand — come.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines NEAR as adjective: nigh; not far distant in place, time, or degree; closely related by blood; present and ready to aid; intimate; dear; close; next to one (opposed to off). Adverb: almost. Verb transitive: to approach. He cites Genesis 27:21, Romans 13:11, Leviticus 18:6, and Isaiah 55:6.
webster_full: NEAR, adjective [This seems to be a contracted word, from nigher, the comparative of neh, nih or nieh; strait, narrow; to narrow]

1. Nigh; not far distant in place, time or degree. Regularly, near should be followed by to, but this is often omitted. We say, a house stands near a river; a friend sits near me; the man fell and was near destruction.
And Jacob went near to Isaac his father. Genesis 27:21.
Now is our salvation nearer than when we believed. Romans 13:11.
2. Closely related by blood.
She is thy fathers near kinswoman. Leviticus 18:6.
3. Not distant in affection, support or assistance; present; ready; willing to aid.
Call upon the Lord, while he is near. Isaiah 55:6.
4. Intimate; united in close ties of affection or confidence; as a near friend.
NEAR, adverb Almost; within a little.
NEAR, verb transitive To approach; to come nearer; as, the ship neared the land; a seamans phrase.
scriptures: But it is good for me to draw near to God: I have put my trust in the Lord GOD, that I may declare all thy works.
Isa 55:6
Seek ye the LORD while he may be found, call ye upon him while he is near:
So likewise ye, when ye shall see all these things, know that it is near, even at the doors.
Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with pure water.
And that, knowing the time, that now it is high time to awake out of sleep: for now is our salvation nearer than when we believed.
corruption_summary: Near is corrupted when God is recast as a supportive presence without holiness, when drawing near is sold as a breathing exercise, and when the nearness of the last days is emptied into calendar panic or calendar denial.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is nearness without the Holy. Psalm 73:28 draws near to God. The age keeps the warmth and drops the LORD. Presence is not a mood board.

The second corruption is Isaiah 55:6 as a self-care window. Call ye upon him while he is near is mercy with a door, not an open-ended spa. Hebrews 10:22 draws near with a true heart, sprinkled from an evil conscience.

The third corruption is Matthew 24:33 as either doomscroll or delay. It is near, even at the doors is the Lord at hand. Romans 13:11 is salvation nearer than when we believed — wake, do not brand the hour.

etymology: Webster 1828 treats CRIED as the preterit and participle of CRY: to utter a loud voice; to call importunately in prayer; to lament; to proclaim. This page fills the KJV-gap past tense of the poor man’s call and the Lord’s loud voice. Companion pages already treat cry, prayer, and christ.
biblical_def: Cried in Scripture is not a performance and not a therapy sob. It is the poor man heard, the distress that reaches the temple, the loud voice of the crucified Christ, and the feast-day invitation. David will not polish the wound: this poor man cried, and the LORD heard him (Psa 34:6). Distress will not stay indoor: in my distress I called upon the LORD, and cried unto my God (Psa 18:6). The depths will not be rebranded as silence: out of the depths have I cried unto thee, O LORD (Psa 130:1). Jesus will not die as a quiet example only: Jesus cried with a loud voice (Mat 27:46). Nor will the feast stay private: Jesus stood and cried, saying, If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink (Joh 7:37). The dictionary therefore keeps cried from becoming either spectacle or suppressed piety. It is the Bible’s way of saying: the voice went up — and God heard.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines CRIED as preterit tense and participle of CRY. CRY, verb intransitive: to utter a loud voice; to call importunately in prayer; to lament; to proclaim; to cry to, to implore. Noun: a loud sound; clamor; the cry of the humble. He cites Genesis 41, Numbers 11, Isaiah 65:14, and Psalms 9:12.
webster_full: CRIED, preterit tense and part. of cry.
CRY, verb intransitive preterit tense and participle passive cried.
1. To utter a loud voice; to speak, call or exclaim with vehemence; in a very general sense.
2. To call importunately; to utter a loud voice, by way of earnest request of prayer.
The people cried to Pharaoh for bread. Genesis 41:1.
The people cried to Moses, and he prayed. Numbers 11:1.
3. To utter a loud voice in weeping; to utter the voice of sorrow; to lament.
But ye shall cry for sorrow of heart. Isaiah 65:14.
To cry to, to call on in prayer; to implore.
CRY, noun A loud voice in distress, prayer or request; importunate call.
He forgetteth not the cry of the humble. Psalms 9:12.

This poor man cried, and the LORD heard him, and saved him out of all his troubles.

In my distress I called upon the LORD, and cried unto my God: he heard my voice out of his temple, and my cry came before him, even into his ears.
And about the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani? that is to say, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?
Joh 7:37
In the last day, that great day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried, saying, If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink.
A Song of degrees. Out of the depths have I cried unto thee, O LORD.
corruption_summary: Cried is corrupted when prayer is recast as emotional release, when the cry of the cross is emptied into abandonment-as-despair, and when public crying is sold as branding.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is the poor man as a content arc. Psalm 34:6 cried, and the LORD heard. The age keeps the tears and drops the hearing. Venting is not petition.

The second corruption is Matthew 27:46 as proof that the Father failed. Jesus cried with a loud voice is the sin-bearer quoting the psalm, not a collapse of the Trinity. The cry is substitution, not cosmic accident.

The third corruption is John 7:37 as a stage. Jesus stood and cried, If any man thirst. The recovery is invitation under authority, not a microphone. Psalm 130:1 is out of the depths — not a brand of vulnerability.

etymology: Webster 1828 treats DIE as verb intransitive: to cease to live; to expire; to be punished with death; in theology, to perish everlastingly; to die to sin. CRIED’s companion past tense here is DIED, the KJV-gap common of Adam’s end and Christ’s once-for-all death. Companion pages already treat death, sin, and christ.
biblical_def: Died in Scripture is not a metaphor for change and not a gentle passing only. It is the wages in Adam, and it is the once death of Christ for sinners. The genealogy will not flatter: Adam lived, and he died (Gen 5:5). The gospel will not wait for the worthy: while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us (Rom 5:8). The cross will not be repeated as theater: in that he died, he died unto sin once (Rom 6:10). Paul will not rank it among tips: Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures (1Co 15:3). The patriarchs will not be recast as having arrived: these all died in faith, not having received the promises (Heb 11:13). The dictionary therefore keeps died from becoming either a wellness transition or a mere biography. It is the Bible’s way of saying: death is real — and Christ died for sins.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines DIE as verb intransitive: to cease to live; to expire; to be punished with death; to come to an end; in theology, to perish everlastingly; to become indifferent to, as to die to sin. He cites Exodus 11:5, Romans 5:7, and 1 Corinthians 15.
webster_full: DIE, verb intransitive

1. To be deprived of respiration, of the circulation of blood, and other bodily functions, and rendered incapable of resuscitation, as animals, either by natural decay, by disease, or by violence; to cease to live; to expire; to decease; to perish; and with respect to man, to depart from this world.
All the first born in the land of Egypt shall die. Exodus 11:5.
2. To be punished with death; to lose life for a crime, or for the sake of another.
Christ died for the ungodly. Romans 5:7.
Christ died for our sins. 1 Corinthians 15:22.
10. In theology, to perish everlastingly; to suffer divine wrath and punishment in the future world.
11. To become indifferent to, or to cease to be under the power of; as, to die to sin.
12. To endure great danger and distress.
I die daily. 1 Corinthians 15:22.

And all the days that Adam lived were nine hundred and thirty years: and he died.

But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.
Rom 6:10

These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
corruption_summary: Died is corrupted when death is recast as transition, when Christ died is emptied into moral example, and when died-in-faith is sold as having already arrived.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is Genesis 5:5 as a gentle fade. And he died is the sentence after the garden, not a sleep-story for children only. The age keeps the years and drops the grave.

The second corruption is Romans 5:8 as inspiration. Christ died for us while we were yet sinners is substitution, not a heroic exit. 1 Corinthians 15:3 is according to the scriptures — not a TED talk.

The third corruption is Hebrews 11:13 as arrival. They died in faith, not having received the promises. The recovery is pilgrimage, not manifestation. Romans 6:10 is died unto sin once; He liveth unto God.

etymology: Webster 1828 treats BROKEN as participle passive of BREAK: parted by violence; rent asunder; infirm; made bankrupt. BREAK is to part by force; to violate a covenant; to crush. This page fills the KJV-gap common of the heart God will not despise, and of cisterns that hold no water. Companion pages already treat heart, spirit, and contrite.
biblical_def: Broken in Scripture is not a brand of fragility and not a license to stay shattered. It is the sacrifice God will not despise, the heart He is nigh unto, the bone that shall not be broken, and the cistern that cannot hold water. David will not offer the uncrushed self: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise (Psa 51:17). The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart (Psa 34:18). He healeth the broken in heart (Psa 147:3). The Passover Lamb will not be managed: a bone of him shall not be broken (Joh 19:36). Apostasy will not be rebranded as innovation: they hewed broken cisterns, that can hold no water (Jer 2:13). The dictionary therefore keeps broken from becoming either an affliction-identity or a discarded vessel with no Healer. It is the Bible’s way of saying: crushed before God — and healed by God.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines BROKEN as participle passive of BREAK: parted by violence; rent asunder; infirm; made bankrupt. BREAK, verb: to part by force; to violate a contract or law; to crush; to tame. He cites Daniel 4:27 among many senses.
webster_full: BRO'KEN, participle passive of break. bro'kn. Parted by violence; rent asunder; infirm; made bankrupt.
BREAK, verb transitive preterit tense broke, [brake.obs.] participle passive broke or broken.
1. To part or divide by force and violence, as a solid substance; to rend apart.
6. To sink; to appall or subdue; as, to break the spirits, or the passions.
13. To violate, as a contract or promise.
14. To infringe or violate, as a law, or any moral obligation.
To break the heart, to afflict grievously; to cause great sorrow or grief; to depress with sorrow or despair.
BREAK, noun A state of being open, or the act of separating; an opening made by force.
scriptures: The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.

Jer 2:13
For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.
He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds.
corruption_summary: Broken is corrupted when a broken heart is recast as a permanent identity, when unbroken bones are emptied of Passover, and when broken cisterns are sold as authentic religion.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is Psalm 51:17 as an aesthetic. A broken and a contrite heart is sacrifice God will not despise — not a bio. The age keeps the shatter and drops repentance.
The second corruption is John 19:36 as trivia. A bone of him shall not be broken is the Lamb, not a medical footnote. The recovery is fulfillment, not symbolism-as-hobby.

The third corruption is Jeremiah 2:13 as self-made hydration. Broken cisterns, that can hold no water are forsaking the fountain. Psalm 147:3 healeth the broken in heart — He binds; you do not curate the leak.
